title: New Thoughts on the Non-Freaked Out Approach to Common Core Literacy https://davestuartjr.com/new-thoughts-on-the-non-freaked-out-approach-to-common-core-literacy/
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart revises his 'non-freaked out' approach to Common Core literacy, a framework built on owning and reducing the standards so students become expert at a few critical things rather than mediocre at every sub-skill. In version 2.0 he argues the elements are not equal: argument and non-cognitive skills become the two 'cupping' elements that hold reading, writing, research and speaking together. He broadens non-cognitive skills beyond grit and self-control to include the KIPP character strengths, growth mindset and Conley's key learning skills. He grounds the whole approach in one goal, the long-term flourishing of students, and dismisses debates about the standards' politics as irrelevant to the students who arrive each fall. Close reading loses its own category and becomes part of purposefully handling complex texts, and research is added as a new 'info-savvy, not tech-savvy' element given the many research-related anchor standards.
points: Stuart's founding move is to reduce the standards: own them, then pick the few elements that matter most so students master them.
Version 2.0 elevates argument and non-cognitive skills as overarching elements that give the other literacy practices their purpose and power.
He states his entire teaching philosophy as promoting students' long-term flourishing and treats political arguments about the Common Core as beside the point for students.
Close reading is folded into purposeful work with complex texts, framed by questions like why this text and why it is the right challenge for these kids.
Research is added as 'info-savvy, not tech-savvy', on the grounds that tech skill is pointless if students cannot navigate and use information.
quotes: On the contrary, I saw that we needed to become students of the standards, learning what they actually say and then doing the critical work of reducing them. In short, we needed to own the standards and figure out which were most important, thus enabling us and our students to become experts at a few critical things rather than mediocre at every last sub-skill.

Argument, as Jerry Graff and Cathy Birkenstein-Graff explain masterfully in “An Immodest Proposal for Connecting High School and College,” is the name of the game in academia. Therefore, the first step to helping more students understand and grow comfortable in academic settings is creating secondary classrooms in which argument is a mega-theme throughout the course.

Before I get into my thinking around the four elements in the middle of the non-freaked out (NFO) approach, it's worth emphasizing that the single, driving goal of everything I do as a teacher is to promote the long-term flourishing of my students. With every single one of the instructional minutes I'm given, I pray the strategies, assignments, and lessons I use do that one thing. That's it.

All these things could or could not be true, but here's the thing: they do not matter a damn to the kids who will walk into my class this September. These kids come to me expecting one thing: to be prepared for life when they walk across the graduation stage.

For one thing, close reading died (didn't you read the obituary?); for another, reading a text closely is just something we do in our attempts to grapple with what a complex text is saying and why that matters.

Somehow I want to get better at teaching kids that being tech-savvy is pointless if you can't sophisticatedly navigate the insane amount of information on the Internet and then do something with that information.
